title: [OPINION] Beyond the clinic: The fight against TB begins in the village

byline: Kenneth Hartigan-Go, Ma. Leonora Irene Celiz, Nathan B. Santos

blocks.text: Imagine a rural barangay where a patient develops pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). The clinician sees cavitary disease; the community sees a father unable to work, a child leaving school, a wife spending savings on transportation, and grandparents becoming caregivers.

Here, TB is more than an infection — it can trigger economic hardship. With the disease continuing to afflict Philippine society, controlling it requires not only clinical science but also responsive governance, social protection, and effective health system stewardship.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recognize that TB is strongly shaped by social determinants such as education, employment, living conditions, and access to essential services. These greatly affect whether people are exposed, diagnosed promptly, and able to complete treatment. As a result, the country’s National Tuberculosis Control Program (NTP) should be judged not only by treatment outcomes, but also by its ability to reach and protect communities most vulnerable to TB.

Led by the Department of Health (DOH), the NTP recognizes community engagement as a pillar of TB elimination. The Philippines has expanded the Directly Observed Treatment Short-course strategy (TB-DOTS) since the late 1990s and achieved high treatment success among patients enrolled in care. Yet these gains have not produced sufficient reductions in TB incidence and mortality. Based on the latest data, the Philippines remains a high-burden country for TB.

The gap between treatment success and population-level impact points to a fundamental problem: many people with TB are never reached by the system. Numerous factors such as delayed diagnosis, under-detection, geographic isolation, transportation costs, stigma, income loss, and treatment interruptions continue to impede care. Strong national policies do not automatically produce effective local implementation and may even expose present weaknesses in the health system. Therefore, more funding does not necessarily mean better health outcomes.

The WHO Health System Strengthening Framework helps explain these shortcomings. Leadership and governance are supported by sound policies, but implementation remains inconsistent. Human resources remain a concern, particularly for barangay health workers (BHWs), who connect communities to formal healthcare but often lack sufficient institutional support. These workers also manage multiple vertical programs, creating competing priorities. Service delivery varies according to the capacity of local facilities, while health financing remains fragmented. Health information systems face incomplete reporting, variable data quality, and limited interoperability. Reports highlight localized interruptions and shortages in first-line anti-TB medicines which expose vulnerabilities in pharmaceutical supply chains.

Furthermore, devolution under the Local Government Code of 1991 adds another layer of complexity. The DOH retains responsibility for national TB policies, including standards, procurement, surveillance, and technical assistance, while local governments carry much of the responsibility for staffing, facility operations, local financing, and service delivery. Authority and accountability are therefore divided. The problem is not necessarily the failure of individual institutions, but inadequate coordination among them.

For frontline workers, especially BHWs and Doctors to the Barrios, TB is rarely considered unimportant. Rather, it competes with numerous urgent health concerns in a resource-constrained primary care system. TB should therefore no longer be treated as a specialist program alone, but as an integrated health system and governance responsibility.

Several approaches can move the country in this direction. TB screening should be institutionalized across clinical services, including primary care initiatives such as YAKAP. Active case finding should be strengthened, particularly in vulnerable and geographically isolated communities. Community-based treatment support can reduce practical barriers that cause treatment interruptions. TB education should be integrated into health professional training, wherein interdisciplinary collaboration becomes routine. Finally, multisectoral accountability must connect commitments and implementation with proper monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

blocks.text: Have years of funding produced results? Yes, but only partially. Investment has strengthened policies, treatment capacity, and community-based programs, but it has not eliminated the structural conditions that sustain transmission.

If an engineer or businessman approached TB, the problem might be framed as systems optimization: improve processes, reduce bottlenecks, allocate resources efficiently, and measure performance. These perspectives are valuable, but insufficient alone. A village perspective reminds us that behind every case is a household whose ability to access and complete care is shaped by social determinants of health.

Ending TB in the Philippines therefore requires more than successfully treating patients one at a time. It requires a health system capable of finding patients early, keeping them in care, and addressing the conditions that allow TB to persist. The NTP has achieved important gains, but the next stage of TB control must move beyond clinical success toward system-wide and community-centered action. The true measure of success is not simply whether treatment works, but whether the village is protected from the social and economic consequences of TB. – Rappler.com

The authors are with the Health Governance Program of the Ateneo Policy Center, School of Government, at Ateneo de Manila University. Dr. Kenneth Y. Hartigan-Go is a senior research fellow, Dr. Ma. Leonora Irene Celiz is from the DOH Doctors to the Barrios Program, and Nathan B. Santos is a research assistant.
